items.item: Tags can be used for retaining important historical snapshots for auditing purposes.
ConcurrentAppendException occurs when a concurrent operation adds files in the same partition your operation reads.

at.step: Reveal: partition writers so conflicts are rare

items.item: Partitioning a table by the same columns used in two operations' conditions can make their file sets disjoint, avoiding the conflict.

at.step: Reveal: partition writers so conflicts are rare

items.item: Every commit is one atomic swap of a single pointer — writers succeed, retry, or fail by touching the same files.

at.step: Reveal: partition writers so conflicts are rare

items.item: A retention policy and a legal-hold tag coexist without changing each other — the tag survives; the rest still expires.
Maintenance is a writer too, and scheduling it against the writers it serves is the design decision, not an afterthought.
A retry doesn't change which files two writers touch — it only repeats the same collision until one gives up.
A new writer's partition overlap should be checked against every existing writer before it ships, not discovered from a production conflict.

at.step: Prove it: a new writer joins the table

items.item: Who may change the schema, and under which review, is a written decision, never a default every writer quietly assumes.

at.step: Reveal: schema evolution as a written decision

items.item: This topic leaves out the commit protocols, snapshot structures, catalog implementations and maintenance procedures, erasure itself, the CDC merge, and the optimistic-versus-pessimistic concurrency theory.
Optimistic concurrency via atomic metadata swap and tag-based retention are established lakehouse practice, not an emerging technique.
This topic gives the shop its concurrent-writer design; the next design is a resumable multi-terabyte historical backfill, the biggest writer the table will see.
Treated as background housekeeping, a maintenance job can starve the very ingest it was supposed to keep tidy for.
